prompt.context: Our client, Dark Sky, is a small manufacturer of unmanned (i.e. remotely piloted) data collection aircraft. Dark Sky produces the Assessor, an aircraft originally designed for unmanned weather exploration. In 2006, the United States military began purchasing Assessors for use in Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance (ISR) missions. The Assessor is profitable, but sales have stagnated and the client wishes to grow.
prompt.question: What are some steps Dark Sky could take to achieve growth?

clarifying_info.a: Dark Sky's only customer is the U.S. Military.

clarifying_info.q: What is the nature of the contract with the military?
clarifying_info.a: Dark Sky has a Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee contract with the U.S. Military for Assessor sales. The contract has been extended in the past and is up for renegotiation; the military has agreed to a marginal fee (price) increase to account for inflation. Contracts for new aircraft will be structured similarly.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current price of the Assessor?
clarifying_info.a: The price of the Assessor has remained constant at $100,000 per unit. The military has agreed to a 10% price increase, bringing it to $110,000 per unit.

clarifying_info.q: Does Dark Sky have capacity to grow?
clarifying_info.a: The firm has additional capacity and is positioned to strengthen any division of the workforce if required (e.g., sales force, manufacturing, R&D).

clarifying_info.q: What products does Dark Sky currently sell?
clarifying_info.a: Dark Sky only sells the Assessor, but has designed prototypes specifically for military operations.

There are approximately 20 competitors that manufacture unmanned aircraft. Though too small to purchase a competitor, Dark Sky has been considered an acquisition target. Dark Sky's lack of growth in recent years concerns potential buyers.

clarifying_info.q: What is special about the Assessor aircraft?
clarifying_info.a: Dark Sky designs a unique aircraft launched from a catapult device; the aircraft can be launched from ships at sea or from harsh terrain (e.g., desert, mountains).

exhibits.title: Revenue ($, Million)
exhibits.shows: A bar or line chart showing Dark Sky's annual revenue from 2004 to 2014 in millions of dollars. Revenue starts near zero around 2004-2005, rises sharply from 2006 onward, and levels off around $5 million by 2010-2014.
exhibits.data: Revenue axis: 0 to 5 ($M); Years shown: 2004, 2006, 2008, 2010, 2012, 2014; Revenue in 2006 appears approximately $0.5M; Revenue in 2010 and 2014 appears approximately $5M

exhibits.title: New Product Sales Forecast, 2015
exhibits.shows: A table showing three new aircraft prototypes (SeaBird, SandBird, JointBird) with projected 2015 unit sales to the Navy and Army, and price per aircraft for each.
exhibits.data: SeaBird: Navy 50 units, Army --, Price $220,000; SandBird: Navy --, Army 60 units, Price $210,000; JointBird: Navy 38 units, Army 52 units, Price $180,000

exhibits.title: Impact of New Product on Assessor Sales
exhibits.shows: A table showing the percentage of Assessor unit sales lost due to cannibalization if each new product is introduced.
exhibits.data: SeaBird: causes 40% cannibalization of Assessor sales; SandBird: causes 70% cannibalization; JointBird: causes 90% cannibalization

framework: Organic growth options: increase penetration of existing military customer, product development (new aircraft models, accessories, training services), new market entry (international markets, domestic non-military: Border Patrol, police, news), diversification into new products for new markets, pricing strategy

External growth options: joint ventures with larger defense firms to expand market access or capability, merger/acquisition targets (or position Dark Sky as attractive acquisition target), partnerships
Opportunity assessment: evaluate each new aircraft prototype (SeaBird, SandBird, JointBird) by 2015 forecasted revenue net of Assessor cannibalization to identify the best short-term growth lever

questions.prompt: (Exhibit 1a) How many units of the Assessor were sold in 2014?
questions.guidance: Candidate should read $5M revenue from the chart and divide by $100K/unit price to derive unit volume.

questions.prompt: (Exhibit 1b) What was the revenue growth rate from 2006 to 2010?
questions.guidance: Candidate should read starting revenue (~$500K in 2006) and ending revenue (~$5M in 2010) and compute percentage growth.

questions.prompt: (Exhibit 2) To maximize short-term revenue growth, which new aircraft should Dark Sky produce?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate total 2015 revenue for each scenario: Assessor revenue (50 units at $110K, cannibalized by the relevant %) plus new product revenue (units x price). The answer is JointBird with the highest total revenue of $16,750,000.

math.setup: Assessor base: 50 units at $110,000 = $5,500,000 with no new product. New Assessor price = $100,000 x 1.10 = $110,000. Cannibalization reduces Assessor units per Exhibit 3.
steps: Assessor units with SeaBird = 50 x (1 - 40%) = 30; Assessor revenue = 30 x $110,000 = $3,300,000
Assessor units with SandBird = 50 x (1 - 70%) = 15; Assessor revenue = 15 x $110,000 = $1,650,000
Assessor units with JointBird = 50 x (1 - 90%) = 5; Assessor revenue = 5 x $110,000 = $550,000
math.answer: JointBird maximizes total 2015 revenue at $16,750,000 vs. $14,300,000 (SeaBird), $14,250,000 (SandBird), $5,500,000 (Assessor only)

brainstorming.prompt: What are the organic and external growth options available to Dark Sky?

categories.name: Organic – Market Penetration
ideas: Negotiate additional Assessor unit purchases with the U.S. Military
Leverage the upcoming contract renegotiation to secure longer-term volume commitments

categories.name: Organic – Product Development
ideas: Develop new unmanned aircraft models tailored for specific military missions (SeaBird, SandBird, JointBird prototypes)
Add aircraft accessories or modular payload capabilities
Offer training services for military operators
Develop maintenance and sustainment service contracts

categories.name: Organic – New Market Entry
ideas: Expand into domestic non-military markets: Border Patrol, police departments, news organizations
Target commercial applications: agriculture, infrastructure inspection, disaster response

categories.name: Organic – Pricing
ideas: Negotiate higher per-unit price increases beyond the agreed 10%
Introduce tiered pricing for different capability levels

categories.name: External – Partnerships & JVs
ideas: Joint venture with a larger defense contractor to access larger military contracts
Contract with a foreign partner to enter international markets
Co-develop next-generation aircraft with a technology partner

categories.name: External – M&A
ideas: Acquire a smaller competitor to gain product mix or capacity
Position Dark Sky as an attractive acquisition target to realize value for shareholders

recommendation: Based on 2015 forecasted revenue, Dark Sky should introduce the JointBird to the U.S. Military. JointBird generates $16,750,000 in total revenue — the highest of all scenarios — by selling to both the Navy (38 units) and Army (52 units) at $180,000 per aircraft, despite high cannibalization of Assessor sales.
In parallel, Dark Sky should pursue other organic growth levers (new market entry, accessories, services) to diversify beyond a single military customer and reduce contract renewal risk.
risks: Heavy cannibalization of Assessor sales (90%) means Assessor-only revenue collapses to $550,000; if JointBird ramp-up is delayed, total revenue could be lower than expected
Cost-plus contract profitability should be verified — if JointBird unit economics are weaker than assumed, the revenue advantage may not translate to profit
Dependence on a single customer (U.S. Military) creates significant concentration risk
Competitive response from ~20 rival unmanned aircraft manufacturers
Is the $550,000 remaining Assessor revenue worth the cost of continuing to produce it?
next_steps: Validate JointBird unit profitability and production cost under Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee terms
Assess production timeline: can Dark Sky begin JointBird manufacturing within the current year?
Explore whether producing multiple new aircraft sequentially (e.g., SandBird then SeaBird) is feasible and what the combined revenue would be
Investigate the potential for new market entry to reduce military customer concentration
Evaluate acquisition interest from larger defense primes as a strategic liquidity option
